brief.head: Marriage, unbundled
brief.text: Two centuries ago marriage bundled sex, companionship, romance, parenthood and friendship, Amit Varma said; recent decades have brought what he calls the great unbundling. {106-C11}

brief.head: Editing grown-ups
brief.text: A friendly virus fixing the mitochondria in muscle cells could cure type 2 diabetes for life, Ajay Shah said. He expects edits not just to embryos but to living adults. {106-C15}

brief.head: Refine it out there
brief.text: Don’t tow asteroids home, Ajay Shah said; that is like hauling a coal mine’s waste. Build robotic factories in the asteroid belt and ship back refined metal. {106-C17}

brief.head: The idle car
brief.text: A self-driving car that moves all day matches a metro’s efficiency, Ajay Shah said, and goes door to door. A privately owned car mostly sits idle. {106-C21}

brief.head: The fertility puzzle
brief.text: Social acceptance of births outside marriage, good childcare and reproductive technology: countries strong on all three, Ajay Shah said, will end up with more children. {106-C22}

thought.text: You can do what you want, but you can’t want what you want.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, bewildered by Amit Varma’s vision of feelings produced on demand

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah look 25 years ahead
lead.head: Forecast now, apologise in 2050
body: Just before the cameras rolled, Ajay Shah confessed to the great tragedy of his life: he has lost his optimism for interstellar travel. Amit Varma, whose worry on most days is getting from Andheri to Bandra, steered them somewhere nearer: the world of 2050.

The question had come a couple of months earlier, from their colleague Vaishnav, on a drive home after dinner: what will the world look like in 30 years? Shah came up with five things on the spot. Varma, who says he has an eagle eye for content, said: episode.

They settled on 2050, 25 years out, a good round figure. Varma set out the caveat first: “When you’re forecasting the future, you often tend to overestimate the short term, underestimate the long term.” {106-C01}
To show how hard it is, he went back 35 years, to 1990, when he was 16, and asked what had changed since.
## Looking back to look ahead
Varma counted three changes: friends found by choice rather than geography, a post-scarcity world of songs, books and films, and everyday magic such as GPS and free video calls.
Shah added that India has caught up with the West in personal consumption. The gap now lies in public goods: cleaner air, better criminal justice, a less dangerous income tax. {106-C05}
## Amit’s five
Varma’s predictions leant on AI, and he warned against judging it by today’s ChatGPT. Artificial general intelligence, he thinks, is about five years away.
By 2050, he said, the algorithm will not just find our entertainment but make it, to suit each person’s tastes and moods. Technology will also learn to produce feelings on demand.
Machines will meet our instrumental needs, leaving human bonds more honest and live art more valued. Relationships will be remapped, and some cities will welcome anyone with a job.
## Ajay’s ten

Shah promised “some more pedestrian things”, and delivered ten. Some were modest: he would like a brain-machine interface that runs regressions in his head and searches his own archive of millions of words.
Others were sweeping. Solar and wind, he said, will push the market price of electricity to zero for hours of the day. {106-C14}
War will be fought by machines, which could make wars easier to end: “If they’re just machines flying and killing machines, then you will expend pressure, but you will not expend blood.” {106-C18}
Meat will come from re-engineered bacteria and algae, and a fertilised egg may become a newborn inside a machine.

Their sharpest disagreement came on climate. Shah expects rises of 2.5 to 3 degrees to be baked in. Varma said he would “vehemently and violently disagree”, and invoked “the great economist Ajay Shah” in his support.
Alarmism, Varma argued, follows funding, and cheap energy and nuclear power will solve the problem. {106-C25}
Shah’s recommendation was a lesson in modesty: John Maynard Keynes’s 1930 essay *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren*, much of which did not work out.
Varma saw bravery in it. Anyone predicting the future, he said, knows they will get it really wrong. “And yet he did it. And yet we did it.”
If the show is still around, their first episode of 2050 will be on what they got wrong.

second.label: Interstellar travel
second.head: Physics let him down
second.deck: Ajay Shah, born in 1966, mourns the breakthroughs his lifetime never brought
body: Alpha Centauri is four and a half light years away, Ajay Shah said, and he sees no way to make the trip in under a thousand years. {#lightyears} That leaves a robotic probe, or humans in a fully self-sustaining ecosystem.

As a young man he treated physics as malleable: surely wormholes, surely ways past the speed of light. Born in 1966, he counts the hundred years before his birth as sparkling, with physics changing how we saw the world every decade. His own life, he said, has been “a wasteland of dull physics”. {106-S01}
Amit Varma was less cosmic. Most days, he said, his worry on leaving home is how to get to Bandra from Andheri. {106-J02}

quote.text: So the great disappointment of my life is this feeling that the physics just never happened.

second.caption: losing hope of interstellar travel

third.head: Talk that came true
body: Long ago, Ajay Shah recalled, Bill Gates said in an interview that voice recognition was coming. Shah was sceptical. “I said, like what? Voice recognition? It’s so difficult. But you know what? Actually the AI happened.” {106-S07}
Gates could not have known which AI was in the pipeline, Shah said. Now he expects it to cope even with “a thick Bengali accent”. Amit Varma: “Unnecessary.”

Hence Shah’s confidence in brain-machine interfaces. He wants regressions in his head, and his archive of millions of words on tap: “I just want my own information delivered back to me because then I ain’t forgetting.” {106-C16}

Varma has composed symphonies in his head since he was seven or eight, but never became a musician: “I was too freaking lazy to learn an instrument.” {106-S08} An interface could finally play his music as he imagines it.
third.caption: Bill Gates’s bet on voice recognition

p2.title: Fifteen bets on 2050
p2.deck: Amit Varma made five predictions and Ajay Shah ten, after a look back at 1990. {106-C01}

sections.label: Looking back
sections.head: Magic we stopped noticing
sections.caption: the world since 1990
body: To forecast 2050 with some humility, Amit Varma first went back 35 years, to 1990, when he was 16, and asked what had changed since. He found three things he could not have seen coming.

The first is communities of choice. Before the internet, friends came from geography: school, college, the workplace. “The surface area of serendipity is low,” he said. {106-C02} Most of his dear friends are people he could not otherwise have met. Even he and Ajay Shah, both in Bombay, would never have crossed paths.

The second is a post-scarcity world in bits and bytes. Making a mixtape, or tracking down a Van Morrison album after hearing one song, was once hard work. Now any song, book or film is a moment away. {106-C03}
## Everyday magic

The third is Arthur C. Clarke’s third law: any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. Never being lost, thanks to GPS, would have seemed utopian in 1990. As a student in the late 1980s, Varma queued at an STD booth outside the Fergusson College hostel in Pune to call his parents. {106-S04} Now he can video-call loved ones anywhere in the world.

~ Shah added the computer revolution, which he thinks people still do not sufficiently appreciate. The phone in our hand, he said, is more powerful than the world’s most powerful supercomputer of twenty years ago. {#supercomputer}

quote.text: many of the things we have normalized and take for granted in our everyday lives are actually magical.

sections.label: Art and feeling
sections.head: Your mood, made to order
sections.caption: entertainment and feelings on demand
body: Amit Varma’s first prediction: by 2050, most of our entertainment will be generated by AI from our preferences. Technology first helped art scale, giving us a Hollywood, a Bollywood and a Tollywood; now it splinters culture into niches. “I predict that the algorithm will even be the creator itself,” he said. {106-C07}

Ajay Shah wondered whether the billions of items already out there might cover every taste, leaving platforms only to find yours. Their game, he said, is all our spare attention: as Netflix executives once put it, “we’re competing with sleep”. {106-J19} Varma insisted that what he wants does not yet exist.
## Feelings on tap

His second prediction followed from the first. Songs, meditation and drugs are all technologies for putting the brain in particular states, and blunt ones. Once AI understands the brain, even as a black box, we could summon peace, focus or happiness directly, and perhaps treat chronic depression or ADHD. {106-C08}
Robert Nozick’s thought experiment, *The Experience Machine*, argued that we would still choose the real world. Nozick is one of Varma’s favourite thinkers, but here he disagrees. {106-R01}
~ Shah foresaw tremendous philosophical challenges. If a button could change how we feel, he said, we would have to decide what we would like to feel. He admitted he would be bewildered. {106-C09}

quote.text: the world is a technology for making us feel a particular way. A song is a machine that makes me feel a particular way.

sections.label: Machines and people
sections.head: Live, and in the flesh
sections.caption: deeper bonds with machines and people
body: Amit Varma’s third prediction: deeper connections with both machines and people. He would welcome an AI companion like the spirit animals of Philip Pullman’s *Northern Lights* trilogy, and a virtual Ajay Shah to give advice “so I can conveniently ignore it”. {106-J05}

If sex dolls and machines meet instrumental needs, he argued, conversations between people can turn to what really matters. He respects lust more than love, because lust is honest; love may be a rationalisation.
## Art in person

Art goes the same way. AI may take away the validation artists get, but not the joy of creating or of live connection. Ticket prices for stand-up shows and concerts, he predicted, will go up. {106-C10}

Shah was in Bombay when Beethoven’s Ninth was first performed in India. “My ears could tell there were flaws in the performance. But the point was that there were people who put it together.” {106-S06}
~ His worry is the money. Live art might end up like a school show, with parents dragged in to applaud: “really the world’s worst hours that any parent has had to spend”. {106-J06}

quote.text: The idea of stand up comedy is not that you tell me a joke which I laugh at. The laughing is not the point.

sections.label: Global cities
sections.head: A job is the only visa
sections.caption: truly global cities
body: Amit Varma’s fifth prediction is truly global cities. If you get a job somewhere, he said, you should be able to go there: no interview, no visa. Migrants from Bihar and UP who drive Mumbai’s taxis make everyone better off.
Dubai, Singapore and the Hong Kong of old show the way, with low taxes and no nationalism. “Openness can be their comparative advantage,” he said. {106-C12}

Ajay Shah sketched a darker version: cosmopolitan cities behind walls, barbarians at the gates, drones on guard. He also cited the pandemic-era digital nomad visas of Estonia and Portugal, which ask only for a stable work-from-home income. But he doubts Dubai: remote workers choose for life, people, weather and culture, “not a hot desert”.
## Money by theorem

Varma expects a global currency, a successor to Bitcoin, which he called “a proto-something”. Shah agreed, for his own reasons. Central banks failed for centuries, he said; only in 1987 did New Zealand get to inflation targeting. {#nz}

~ In a Trump world, can the US Fed be trusted? World GDP, Shah said, is too big to rest on one country’s fragile institutions. Crypto today has grifters and Trump coin, but he expects 25 years of real innovation. {106-C13}

quote.text: if you can remove frail human institutions and replace them by cold theorems and algorithms, then you’ve added value to the world.

sections.label: Cheap power
sections.head: Sunshine on the house
sections.caption: free electricity
body: Nuclear power was once sold as energy too cheap to meter. Ajay Shah, as an economist, said hold your horses: the plants are extremely expensive hardware, with high capital costs.

The dominant force, he said, is solar and wind, riding experience curves through small gains. He had just read that an undergraduate had solved the equations of windmill blades better, for gains of 1 or 2 per cent. {#windmill}
India’s best wind sites, he noted, are offshore beyond Tamil Nadu and in a ring around Sri Lanka. {#offshore}
## Free for hours

With cheap batteries and time-of-day pricing, power will be dear in the evening but free in the sunny hours. What would we do, he asked, if electricity were free for significant chunks of the day? {106-C14}
His trivial example: desalinate seawater all along the coast in those hours. And nobody in their good mind in India, he said, should be putting up fossil-fuel capacity.
~ Amit Varma pointed listeners to their episode on the future of electricity, one of the show’s best in his view, and to the one on nuclear power.

quote.text: I’m saying we have not confronted the staggering consequences of the word zero.

sections.label: The disagreement
sections.head: Two degrees of separation
sections.caption: climate change
body: Ajay Shah is optimistic about renewables but gloomy about the air. Carbon dioxide, he said, takes about a thousand years to go away, so the stock matters, not just today’s emissions. {#co2}

We are at about 1.5 degrees of warming over pre-industrial times, roughly as the models predicted, and the oceans delay the full effect by 20 to 40 years. “So I think two point five or three degree rises in the temperature are kinda baked in.” {106-C24}

The world once fixed the ozone layer by phasing out CFCs, he recalled, and India did not demand 20 more years of Freon. Without American leadership, he sees no such deal on carbon, which needs a commensurate tax. {106-S11}
## The dissent

Amit Varma agreed that warming is real and caused by humans, but said it is less severe than claimed and will be solved. Climate NGOs, he argued, are funded for predicting dystopia, so they exaggerate. {106-C25}
He cited Al Gore’s failed ten-year forecasts, Bjorn Lomborg’s books and France, which is 71 per cent nuclear and emits a tenth of the world average carbon dioxide per kilowatt hour. {#france}
~ Shah’s own picture of 2050 is of people sheltering inside steel structures, keeping the weather out.

quote.text: That kind of global coordination is no longer available. We no longer have American leadership.

side.boxText: In 1930 John Maynard Keynes wrote *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren*. Ajay Shah’s recommendation: one of the smartest people in history tried hard to foresee productivity, and much of it did not work out. A lesson for futurists. {106-R12}

contQuote.text: When we read these books, we are not just speculating on something that is in the future and may or may not happen. We are speculating on the present because the future is here.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From a Russian airfield to Tolstoy’s dining room, and what each teaches

stories.start: This is one of the most audacious and innovative and brilliant attacks
stories.end: hundred others will think, Oh, how cool, can I do
stories.caption: Ukraine’s drone raid on Russia’s bombers
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Ukraine’s raid on Russia’s strategic bombers
stories.head: The day the truck roofs opened
body: Ajay Shah called it “one of the most audacious and innovative and brilliant attacks in the history of warfare”, and walked through how Ukraine pulled it off. {106-S10}
First, 117 drones with explosive payloads of perhaps 3 to 5 kg were smuggled into Russia, probably across the Chinese or Kazakh border, where checking is low.
In a safe house, reportedly right next to an FSB building, they were assembled and loaded into containers on trucks. The tops of the containers could retract.

Unwitting Russian drivers were told to take the trucks to set GPS coordinates and step out. They dutifully followed Google Maps to four or five bases. Five to ten kilometres from the airfields, the roofs opened.

The drones flew at about 50 km an hour, the peak speed of birds, so defenders took time to tell what they were. {#fiftykph} They used the ordinary 4G network over a VPN home, and the crews were already safely inside Ukraine.

Ukraine claims 41 strategic bombers and AWACS planes destroyed, worth about $7 billion; independent estimates confirm 21. If the 41 is right, about 34 per cent of Russia’s strategic bomber fleet is gone. Many of these aircraft are no longer made, and Russia lacks the factories to make them.
The bill, by Shah’s rough reckoning: two lakh dollars of drones, about $2 million all in. {#twomillion}
~ Then the fear. “It’s like 9-11,” Shah said. Once it has been done, the genie is out of the bottle.
stories.why: A few million dollars destroyed billions in assets that cannot be replaced. Amit Varma’s worry is darker: cheap drone swarms could hit a crowd in Mumbai, and the future of war may become the future of terror. {106-C19}
stories.postscript: Varma noted that such an attack was unimaginable and unimplementable as little as three years ago, born of necessity in an existential war. {#threeyears}

stories.start: there's a great story about Leo Tolstoy I like telling
stories.end: And that's a difference that we have in our heads.
stories.caption: Tolstoy’s chicken
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a vegetarian host and meat without killing
stories.head: Aunt orders chicken, gets one
body: Leo Tolstoy was by then a vegetarian, Amit Varma said, when his aunt announced that she would come to dinner and eat chicken and nothing else. {106-S09}
She came. In the dining room she found a live chicken on her chair. You want a chicken, Tolstoy told her: here it is. Kill it, cook it, then eat it.

Varma once wrote an essay called *Tolstoy’s Chicken*, so long ago that it no longer exists. He loves meat and thinks it necessary for health, but dislikes the thought of being responsible for killing animals.
~ Lab-grown meat would end that dilemma for him. Ajay Shah’s reason to expect it by 2050: “it’s cheaper to get an E. coli to make a muscle cell than to grow a cow or a goat.” {106-C20}

quote.text: the difference between the chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.

stories.postscript: Varma also cited Matt Ridley’s speculation that Homo sapiens ate Neanderthals, and wondered whether human meat could be grown in a lab. {106-J23}

stories.start: In the late eighties, I caught a plane and I went to the United States
stories.end: To step into LAX you felt like this was a science fiction city.
stories.caption: his first CD, in America
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on landing in America in the late 1980s
stories.head: All the theory, none of the CDs
body: In the late 1980s Ajay Shah caught a plane to Los Angeles to do a PhD; by then, flying was standard. Montek Ahluwalia, he recalled, had been among the last cohorts to go to study in Britain by boat from Bombay, up the Red Sea. {106-S02}
“In the late 80s, India was truly backward,” Shah said. His middle-class parents were early adopters of every new thing, yet America was full of firsts.
He saw his first CD player and his first CD. “I read innumerable issues of IEEE Spectrum, and I was a complete enthusiast about CDs, but I’d never touched a CD before.” {106-S03}
~ He saw dahi sold in boxes, when Indians always made their own at home, and highways at 100 kph. Stepping into LAX felt like entering a science fiction city.
stories.why: Then, going abroad made India feel backward. Today, Shah said, the Indian elite consume at the global state of the art; the West’s lead is in public goods, such as cleaner air and better criminal justice. {106-C05}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s reply: “We had CD bars in India on the highways.”

stories.start: I will for a moment go back to chess and what happened
stories.end: So it's actually uh you know made that whole field uh richer.
stories.caption: how AI made chess richer
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the machines really did to chess
stories.head: Engines broke the Soviet mould
body: When engines grew stronger than the world’s best player, Amit Varma said, everyone assumed chess was solved and would die, or turn into memorising computer lines, with everyone playing alike. Exactly the opposite happened.

Before, nearly everybody played in one style, built on the Soviet school’s shared heuristics. “AI allowed you to find concrete exceptions to abstract principles that were in general good,” Varma said. {106-S05}
Many players also learned straight from the machines, not from the same books and circuits. Hence Wesley So, Nakamura and Giri, whose styles differ sharply from one another.
~ Games now pair deeper preparation with more original play over the board, as players lure opponents into second- and third-best lines they have not prepared.
stories.why: Machines can deepen human engagement instead of replacing it. That is Varma’s model for 2050: let machines meet instrumental needs, and human relationships and live art grow more honest and more valued. {106-C10}

quiz.q: Which law, cited by Amit Varma, says advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic?
quiz.a: Arthur C. Clarke’s third law, which he applied to GPS and video calls.

quiz.q: How big a market for computers did IBM’s Thomas Watson foresee, as Varma quoted him?
quiz.a: A world market for three computers at most: a warning about judging early AI.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah think robotic warfare could make wars easier to stop?
quiz.a: Only machines are destroyed, so no blood is spilt and battlefield facts become clear.

quiz.q: What simple use did Shah suggest for hours when India’s electricity costs nothing?
quiz.a: Desalinating seawater all along the coast to produce very large supplies of water.

quiz.q: Which global problem did the world once solve together, and why does Shah doubt a repeat?
quiz.a: The ozone layer, by phasing out CFCs; American leadership is no longer available.

quiz.q: What Unix command did Ajay Shah want to run on his own brain?
quiz.a: Grep, a tool for searching text files, like a menu for steaks.
